status_summary: The Fed and the other bank regulators have taken several agency-level steps in the direction the chapter describes. The Board announced its withdrawal from the Network for Greening the Financial System on 2025-01-17 (before the inauguration), said on 2025-06-23 that reputational risk would leave its examination programs, and joined the FDIC and OCC on 2025-10-16 in withdrawing the 2023 climate risk principles for large banks (rescission notice published 2025-11-18). The Board proposed on 2026-02-26 to codify the reputational-risk change; the OCC and FDIC finalized a parallel rule effective 2026-06-09, and no final Board rule was found. The statutory piece the chapter names, amending the Fed's financial stability mandate, has no action found. The agencies describe the period's capital-framework changes, such as the enhanced supplementary leverage ratio rule published 2025-12-01, as recalibrations (Inference: whether these amount to the chapter's call to focus regulation on capital adequacy is a judgment).

timeline.event: Federal Reserve Board announces its withdrawal from the Network for Greening the Financial System, saying the network's work had broadened beyond the Board's statutory mandate (announced three days before the inauguration).
Trade press reports, citing a media report with unnamed sourcing, that the Fed disbanded several internal climate committees; the Fed's own confirmation was not found.
Board announces that reputational risk will no longer be a component of its examination programs and begins removing references from supervisory materials.

Fed, FDIC and OCC announce withdrawal of the interagency climate-related financial risk principles for large institutions, effective immediately; the agencies say existing safety and soundness standards already cover material risks.
Federal Register notice of the rescission of the climate principles is published (90 FR 51756), effective the same day.

Fed, FDIC and OCC publish a final rule changing the enhanced supplementary leverage ratio for the largest banks, effective 2026-04-01; the agencies describe it as a recalibration so the ratio acts as a backstop to risk-based capital.
Board proposes a rule to codify the removal of reputation risk from its supervision and to bar pressuring banks over lawful but politically disfavored activities; comments closed 2026-04-27.
OCC and FDIC publish a final rule removing reputation risk from their supervision, effective 2026-06-09. The Board is not a party to this rule.

The Federal Reserve Board, FDIC and OCC announce updates to certain interagency documents removing references to reputation risk, complementing their earlier steps ending its use in supervision; the release does not list the documents or a Federal Register citation.

title: Focus Fed regulation on bank capital adequacy and bar ESG and climate factors
uncertainties: Stage is a judgment: the climate and reputation-risk steps match the ESG half of the recommendation, but the statutory amendment is absent and the capital half is ambiguous (the 2025-12-01 leverage rule and the 2026-10-02 stress test transparency final rule, effective 2026-11-02, are capital-framework changes that the agencies describe as recalibrations; whether they reflect a refocus on capital adequacy is a characterization, not a fact). The disbanding of Fed climate committees rests on a media report with unnamed sourcing; one law-firm summary dates it to March 2025, and the Fed's confirmation was not found. The NGFS withdrawal was announced before 2025-01-20, so it is context rather than an action of the current term. The Board's adoption date for the climate rescission is not stated in the notice. Federal Register queries through 2026-10-13 and the Board's 2026 press release list show no final Board reputation-risk rule; the 2026-06-02 interagency release does not name the documents changed. The NCUA adopted its own reputation-risk final rule (Federal Register, 2026-06-25), a parallel action by another regulator that is not part of this Fed record. Congress.gov was not checked for bills on the financial stability mandate.
